English: Deepfakes and AI-generated content
What is it?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that learns patterns from very large amounts of data and then uses those patterns to predict, sort or create. Generative AI creates new content — a paragraph, a picture, a song or a video — from a short instruction. A deepfake is a photo, video or audio clip made or altered with AI so that a real person seems to say or do something they never did. The word joins “deep learning” (the AI method) and “fake”.

In early 2024, an employee of a multinational firm's Hong Kong office joined a video call with people who looked and sounded like the company's finance chief and colleagues. On their instructions he made a series of transfers worth about US$25 million. Every other person on the call was a deepfake. Lesson: seeing a familiar face on a live call is no longer proof. Large or unusual requests must be confirmed through a separate, known channel.
The technology is neutral. Consent, labelling and intent make the difference between creative work and a crime.
AI-generated images, videos and voices
What is it?

AI can now produce a photograph of a person who does not exist, swap one face onto another in a video, make a real person's lips match new words (lip-sync), and clone a voice from a short sample so that it can say anything typed into it. Some clues can reveal manipulation, especially in quickly made fakes. But tools improve every month, and a good fake may show no clue at all. Clues raise suspicion; they do not prove anything either way.

Detection tools: useful, but not a judge

Online “deepfake detectors” give a percentage such as “72% AI”. Treat this as one clue. Detectors can be wrong both ways, can be fooled by compression on WhatsApp, and are not accepted as proof by themselves. A call- back, the original source or a fact-check carries far more weight.

What is it?

False information ranges from honest mistakes to deliberate campaigns. It spreads fastest when it triggers fear, anger or pride, and when it arrives from someone we trust. In India, false forwards have caused panic during health emergencies and disasters, and have even led to mob violence.

Impersonation and manipulated media
What is it?

Impersonation means pretending to be someone else — through a fake profile using their photos, a hijacked account, or AI media of their face or voice. Morphing is editing a person's photo, often onto a sexual image, to shame or blackmail them. Sextortion is threatening to share intimate or morphed images unless the victim pays or sends more images. The person shown is a victim, whether the image is real or fake. Shame keeps victims silent, which is exactly what the criminal relies on.

What the law and platforms provide

Under the IT Rules 2021, platforms must act on a complaint about intimate or morphed images of a person within 24 hours. Publishing such material is an offence under the IT Act 2000 (ss. 66E, 67, 67A; s. 67B for children) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023; impersonation online is an offence under IT Act s. 66D. Child sexual material is reported at once; it is never copied or viewed (Modules 5 and 7).

Ayesha, 22, received a message with a morphed image made from her public Instagram photos and a demand for ₹5,000. A friend trained as a First Responder told her it was not her fault, helped her save the account link and chat, used StopNCII to create a hash of the image on her own phone, reported the account and filed on cybercrime.gov.in. The account was removed; no payment was made.
AI-based cyber threats and phishing
What is it?

Criminals use AI to make old scams more convincing: cloned voices of relatives, flawless phishing messages in any language, deepfake adverts of celebrities and business leaders promoting trading apps, and live face-swap video calls pretending to be police or company officials. The defence is the same as in Module 2 — check the request, not the polish — plus one new habit: verify through a channel you already trust.

Responsible AI: the consent rule

Creating AI images, video or voice of a real person without their consent can violate their privacy and dignity and may be an offence. Under the DPDP Act 2023, a person's image and voice are personal data. Label AI-generated content you share, never use AI to sexualise, mock or impersonate a real person, and never feed someone else's private photos into an AI tool.
